title: Arjuna Asks Krishna to Repeat the Gita
subtitle: Krishna offers the Anugita in its place
story:
Years later, when people asked what Krishna and Arjuna spoke of in the days after the war, the answer began with a confession: everything Krishna had told him on the battlefield, Arjuna had forgotten.

The war was over. Arjuna had recovered his kingdom and was spending his days in pure joy, doing nothing but keeping company with Krishna in the palace at Hastinapura, in rooms that seemed a piece of heaven, surrounded by relatives and attendants. And yet one thing had begun to trouble him. One day, as the two friends wandered together through that beautiful mansion, Arjuna turned to Krishna. It was on the approach of battle, he said, that Krishna's greatness had become known to him; on that field he had also seen Krishna's form as the Lord of the universe. But everything Krishna had spoken to him then, out of affection, had slipped away from him, because of the fickleness of his mind. He had been curious about those truths again and again, he said — and Krishna would soon be leaving for Dwaraka. Would Krishna tell him once more?

Krishna embraced him before he answered. It was exceedingly disagreeable to him, he said, to learn that Arjuna had not, from folly, received what was imparted. The recollection of all he had told him on that occasion would not come to him now; that teaching was more than sufficient for understanding Brahma, and he could not discourse on it again in detail, for he had spoken of Supreme Brahma while concentrated in yoga. But then his voice softened into a promise: he would recite an old history upon the same topic, and if Arjuna listened with an understanding shaped by his teaching, he might yet attain the highest end.

And so Krishna began the old history. Once, he said, a Brahmana had come to them from the regions of Heaven, from the presence of the Grandsire, a being of irresistible energy, and they had reverenced him duly. When they asked him about the religion of Emancipation — asked, the Brahmana observed, out of compassion for all creatures and not for his own good — he agreed to speak, asking only that they listen with concentrated attention.

The old history concerned a Brahmana named Kasyapa, foremost of all persons conversant with duties. Kasyapa had heard of another Brahmana, one who had become conversant with all the mysteries of religion. This second sage had mastered all the knowledge the scriptures teach about the departure and reappearance of beings, and possessed that direct knowledge of all things which yoga gives. He was skilled in the truths of every topic relating to the world; he knew the truth about pleasure and pain, understood the distinctions between merit and demerit, and had beheld the ends attained by embodied creatures high and low in consequence of their acts. He lived like one already emancipated, crowned with ascetic success and perfectly tranquil, all his senses under complete control. He seemed to blaze with the resplendence of Brahma, could go everywhere at will, and knew the science of disappearing at will from before the eyes of all. He roved in the company of invisible Siddhas and celestial musicians, conversing with them in spots retired from the bustle of humanity, and he was as unattached to all things as the wind.

Kasyapa, having heard of him truly, desired to see him. The foremost of Brahmanas approached the sage, and when he had seen all those wonderful attributes he fell with a rapt heart at the sage's feet, filled with wonder, and began to wait upon that master with dutiful reverence.

So Krishna spoke, in the palace of celestial beauty, with Arjuna before him — and the old history he had promised, the tale the Brahmana of Heaven told to Kasyapa, would unroll through the days that followed into the teaching known as the Anugita.
reflection: Krishna's answer to forgotten truth is not a repetition but a story: he cannot summon back the words of the Gita, so he begins an old history, and the Anugita is born from that refusal. Arjuna's fickleness of mind becomes, in a strange way, the occasion for the teaching to be given again in a new form.
tradition_note: The Anugita is the Mahabharata's own sequel to the Gita, and within the text Krishna explains that he cannot repeat the original discourse; the full old history unfolds through the chapters of the Anugita Parva that follow.
next_story_tease: Before long, Krishna would speak his final teaching to a different disciple, at the foot of an ashvattha tree.
hero_scene: In a palace chamber like a piece of heaven, Krishna embraces Arjuna and begins to speak, while Arjuna — who has just confessed that he forgot everything Krishna taught him on the battlefield — listens with bowed head.
visual_elements: the radiant palace at Hastinapura, crowded with relatives and attendants
Krishna and Arjuna seated close together
Arjuna with head bowed, confessing his forgetfulness
Krishna's hand raised as he begins the old history
